items.title: 68003_Eddie Sauter oral history interview
items.q: I worked with people like that; Robert Emmet Dolling was one

ctx.x: I heard A Little Night Music was that way too. I think you have to give Sondheim his due, and I never know how much goes to the orchestrator and how much goes to composer. It depends really on the guy who does--I use that word advisedly, because most Broadway writers are not composers; they're tunesmiths. There is a huge difference. But Sondheim, not having worked with him, I really don't know. I have a suspicion that he watches his notes carefully.

I worked with people like that; Robert Emmet Dolling was one, and he translated his setting, he made his--even their orchestral settings--we were talking about this sort of thing before, about Hollywood,

how people would give a melody line and they would work it out according to the film. They'll give a breakdown of the film and say you do it. That guy then is the composer, the guy who gave the notes, although he is not composing at all. It's being an executor.
